background.definition: Anterior uveitis is defined as inflammation of the anterior portion (iris and anterior chamber) of the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, and choroid) of the eye. Inflammation confined to the iris and anterior chamber is called iritis. Inflammation of the iris, anterior chamber, and adjacent ciliary body is called iridocyclitis.The terms anterior uveitis, iritis, and iridocyclitis are often used synonymously. Inflammation of the posterior uveal tract is called posterior uveitis. Acute anterior uveitis is defined as less than 6 weeks duration and chronic when greater than 6 weeks.

Since anterior uveitis is associated with many infections, it is suspected that an immune reaction directed against the antigens may cause injury to the uveal tract.

Anterior uveitis is also associated with several autoimmune diseases and a hypersensitivity reaction likely due to the immune complex deposition within the uveal tract. The exact cause of uveitis has not been found to explain the majority of cases.

list.listitem: Patients typically present with acute unilateral, painful red eye complaining of blurred vision, photophobia, and excessive tearing.
Chronic anterior uveitis causes few, if any acute symptoms.

Other associated complaints indicative of anterior uveitis include other nonocular symptoms such as low back pain and stiffness, polyarthritis, nonspecific urethritis, low-grade fever, diarrhea, abdominal cramps and pain, and/or genital ulcerations.
Physical exam findings commonly include decreased visual acuity in the affected eye, an intense conjunctival injection around the limbus, and direct and consensual photophobia.
Extraocular movement is usually normal, while intraocular pressure may be normal or slightly decreased acutely.
Laboratory workup may be unnecessary if uveitis occurs in setting of known systemic disease or in patients taking medicines known to cause uveitis (e.g., rifabutin).

An initial occurrence of uveitis that is unilateral and nongranulomatous (absence of large "mutton fat" keratic precipitates in anterior chamber during slit-lamp exam) with an otherwise unremarkable history and physical requires no additional laboratory workup.

Consider additional testing for recurrent, bilateral, or granulomatous uveitis, including CBC, ESR, ANA, tests for syphilis, PPD with anergy panel, and chest radiograph to rule out sarcoidosis, syphilis, tuberculosis, and herpes simplex/varicella-zoster. Additional testing should be guided by specific etiologies suspected from the history and physical examination to minimize false positive results. For example, SLE is a rare cause of uveitis (<0.5%), with a positive predictive value of routine ANA testing of only 2.9%.

Suspect iritis in a patient presenting with a unilateral, painful red eye complaining of photophobia, blurred vision, and tearing. Rule out other more common causes of the painful red eye, including conjunctivitis, corneal abrasions and ulcers, and foreign bodies.
Slit-lamp examination of the anterior chamber is strongly recommended; consider additional testing to rule out sarcoidosis, syphilis, tuberculosis, and herpes simplex/varicella-zoster.
Strongly consider ophthalmologic consultation before beginning therapy. C
Cycloplegic or mydriatic eye drops are recommended; topical steroids may also be effective. C
If adverse reactions to corticosteroid eye drops are suspected, consider indomethicin drops. B

Severe anterior uveitis not responding to maximal topical steroids may improve with periocular or intravitreal steroid injection or with steroid surgical implants. Adverse events include cataract progression and elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP). C
A tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor such as infliximab is recommended for patients with serous non-infectious uveitis.B

Cycloplegic eye drops (scopolamine, 0.25% BID, for mild to moderate inflammation and atropine, 1% BID to QID, for severe inflammation) and corticosteroids (prednisolone acetate 1%, one drop every 1-6 hours depending on severity, or rimexolone 1%) are recommended for most patients based on results of uncontrolled case series and clinical experience. A comparison of loteprednol 0.5% with prednisolone 1% in 245 patients found that the former was somewhat less effective.

A tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor is recommended for patients with serous non-infectious uveitis. A trial randomized 330 patients with non-infectious sight threatening uveitis to adlimumab or infliximab. Infliximab had a lower relapse rate at 6 months (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.36-.77).
A Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating the efficacy and safety of topical mydriatics in addition to topical steroids for traumatic iridocyclitis.

If corticosteroid eye drops are not tolerated, indomethicin 1% drops may be considered. An RCT of 49 patients found a better early response with the corticosteroid drops but no difference after 14 days.

Severe anterior uveitis not responding to maximal topical steroids may improve with periocular repository steroids (triamcinolone 20-40 mg given as a subtenon injection). Other options include intravitreal steroid injection or steroid surgical implants. Adverse events include cataract progression and elevated IOP, which themselves may require subsequent treatment.
Ciprofloxacin is not effective for anterior uveitis.
Rheumatologic referral for immunosupressive therapy (e.g., methotrexate, adalimumab) and/or systemic steroids may be necessary with bilateral severe uveitis.

A systematic review evaluating the efficacy and safety of immunomodulatory therapies for steroid-refractory anterior uveitis found weak evidence, based on 13 small RCTs with significant methodological shortcomings, that methotrexate, cyclosporine A, azathioprine, adalimumab, and golimumab may be effective in preventing flares, decreasing ocular inflammation, improving visual acuity, and decreasing the use of systemic corticosteroids.
Treat secondary glaucoma with aqueous humor suppressants (not pilocarpine or prostaglandins); consult ophthalmologist for specific recommendations.
Treatment of the underlying systemic condition may also be effective for achieving remission of anterior uveitis in resistant cases.

A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 145 patients with acute anterior uveitis found a possible visual acuity benefit in patients given vitamin C (500 mg) plus vitamin E (100 mg) twice daily. However, there was no difference in laser cell/flare measurements.
Immediate referral to an ophthalmologist is recommended when the diagnosis is uncertain, especially before initiating steroid therapy.
Follow-up ophthamologic care within 24 hours is highly recommended for guidance with tapering cycloplegics and steroids.
When systemic disease is suspected or confirmed, referral to an appropriate medical specialist for treatment may be helpful.

The number and frequency of recommended follow-up visits vary depending on the severity of disease. Mild disease should be seen every 4 to 7 days, moderate disease seen every 2 to 4 days, and those with severe disease seen every 1 to 2 days. C
Visual acuity, slit-lamp, and tonometry exams should be performed for guidance with tapering treatment. C
